draft.briefing: Hey, you're at Lalbagh! Hyder Ali started this botanical garden in 1760, and it sits on rock that's around 3,000 million years old.
draft.hungryLine: VV Puram Food Street is a 10 minute walk, with over 20 pure vegetarian stalls packed into less than 150 metres.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Lal Bagh is a 19 minute walk, Gandhi Bazaar is 16 minutes away, and Bugle Rock is about 20 minutes on foot.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find a bench by the lake in Lal Bagh, next to the big rock with Kempegowda II's watchtower.
moodReplies.surprise-me: Lal Bagh has one of the best exposures of Peninsular Gneiss, and it was declared a National Geological Monument in 1975.

legends.title: The sunset bugle
legends.body: It's said a sentry on Bugle Rock would blow a bugle at sunset and hold up a torch. The three other watchtowers could see it, so people knew the city was safe.

tips.title: Time it for a flower show.
tips.body: Lal Bagh holds flower shows in the weeks of Republic Day (26 January) and Independence Day (15 August).

tips.title: Come back for the Avarekai Mela.
tips.body: Every December or January, VV Puram Food Street cooks up dishes with fresh hyacinth beans bought straight from farmers.

story.title: Old as the earth
story.body: Bugle Rock is a rise of peninsular gneiss with an assessed age of about 3,000 million years.

story.title: Kempegowda's towers
story.body: Kempe Gowda II, who came to power in 1585, built four watchtowers to mark Bangalore's limits, including one on Bugle Rock in the south.

story.title: Hyder Ali's garden
story.body: Hyder Ali laid out Lalbagh, the red garden, during the Sultanate of Mysore. British superintendents later ran it.

story.title: The glass house
story.body: A central glass house went up in 1890 and was used for flower shows.

story.title: The metro arrives
story.body: Lalbagh, South End Circle and National College metro stations all opened on 18 June 2017.
